item.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
item.description: The DOJ's embrace of fair use for AI training breaks with the White House's own framework, as OpenAI, Microsoft and news groups battle over copyright.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

item.title: Massachusetts sues Trump admin to stop ICE's courthouse arrests: 'Unnecessary fear'
item.description: Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration over ICE's courthouse arrests without judicial warrants, saying they violate a new state law.
item.content:encoded:
Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration on Monday to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from carrying out civil arrests in the state's courthouses, arguing that such arrests without judicial warrants are illegal under state law.

The lawsuit filed by Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell challenges a 2025 ICE directive that authorizes agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants, which she says violates the PROTECT Act, a new state law passed ​by the Democratic-led legislature that prohibits civil immigration arrests in state courthouses without judicial warrants. The courthouse protections took effect Nov. 3.

Campbell said the ICE directive interferes with the state's authority to operate its judicial system, disrupts court proceedings, undermines constitutional principles and public safety and spreads fear, chaos and confusion.

"The Massachusetts PROTECT Act makes it illegal for ICE to conduct civil arrests in our courthouses without a judicial warrant. ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable," Campbell said in a statement.

DOJ SUES TO STOP OHIO COURT BLOCKING COURTHOUSE ARRESTS

"ICE is misleading the public by suggesting that these arrests make us safer when, in fact, ICE's actions are preventing criminal cases from moving forward, denying a victim’s ability to obtain accountability, violating a defendant’s due process, and leaving open the possibility that someone facing serious criminal charges could ultimately be released from ICE custody without their criminal case ever being resolved," she continued.

The attorney general said more than 1,110 people have been arrested at her state's courthouses since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, including more than 600 people in 2025 and more than 500 during the first 10 months of 2026.

Campbell said ICE has ignored the new state law and arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants in the two and a half weeks since the courthouse protections went into effect.

"I, along with our district attorneys, share the goal of holding defendants accountable for crimes, yet ICE’s unlawful tactics to arrest someone for a civil immigration violation is not the same as holding them accountable for a crime," Campbell said.

FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS

Campbell said that ICE's courthouse arrests have continued in Massachusetts despite a federal ruling handed down in June by U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in California that vacated the Trump administration's courthouse arrest policy ​in a separate class action lawsuit.

In Monday's lawsuit, Campbell argues the ICE policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act since it was adopted without taking into account the impact it would have on states and because the Immigration and Nationality Act does not explicitly authorize courthouse arrests.

The lawsuit also alleges that the ⁠policy violates the U.S. Constitution's Tenth Amendment, which protects states' rights to maintain authority over their own judicial systems.

"The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety. When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe," Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement. "We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

In a statement to Reuters, a DHS spokesperson argued that making immigration arrests at courthouses "conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already ​know where a target will ​be," adding that "the ability of law enforcement ⁠to make arrests of criminal illegal aliens in courthouses is common sense."

A similar lawsuit against ICE arrests at state courthouses was filed in October by California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

item.title: Trump's Nixon-to-China moment: There's an immigration move only he can make
item.description: President Trump floated immigration on "Saturday in America," and this column argues his pardon power could shield illegal immigrants from deportation.
item.content:encoded:
"Maybe we could touch the subject of immigration." That was President Trump’s suggestion to host Kayleigh McEnany during his Nov. 21 appearance on Fox News’ "Saturday in America."

If the president deploys his power of pardon for a defined class of illegal immigrants, it will be a "golden touch" for them that will enshrine his memory among their communities and add another achievement of enormous significance to his already lengthy column of them.

Such an act of presidential mercy would be unprecedented—without a parallel mass grant of grace in American history—and it would be approved of by supermajorities of Americans and certain to be counted among his greatest achievements as president by citizens of all political persuasions who have long desired an actual breakthrough on this stalemated front.

TRUMP AND IMMIGRATION REFORM: WILL DEMOCRATS MAKE HIM AN OFFER HE CAN'T REFUSE?

The president’s carefully phrased suggestion to McEnany is a good topic for a Thanksgiving dinner conversation: "What should we as a country do about or to the country’s illegal immigrant population?"

Frame the question this way:

"What do we think about a presidential pardon for, say, the 10% of the illegal immigrant population, people whom everyone here could agree ought to be left alone and free of the fear of deportation?"

The best studies estimate the population of illegal immigrants in the country at between 15 and 20 million. Some crossed the border right up to the day President Trump returned to office, but very few have arrived in the country since the spring of 2025. Trump sealed the southern border, and it remains, for all practical purposes, shuttered. "The Wall" has now been built over more than 750 miles. Another 600 miles of wall are planned between now and the end of Trump’s second term. The Border Patrol is funded through the end of Sept. 2029.

President Trump delivered on his promise to close the border.

On Nov. 8, after being asked by Ross Douthat of "60 Minutes" about deportation policy in the past two years, the president said, "I think it was too tough." President Trump then added, "I think it might be too tough, yeah."

TRUMP CAN FINALLY DELIVER THE IMMIGRATION BARGAIN REAGAN WAS PROMISED

His explanation was straightforward.

Some of the election results on Nov. 3 were "because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally."

"Now, there is a large part of the country that thinks that they should be put out," he added. "And there's a large part of the country that thinks that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."

So, what should be done? What should President Trump do?

FOX NEWS POLL: MAJORITY SAYS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT HAS CROSSED THE LINE

Democratic leaders in Congress have a wide-open door to the Oval Office to negotiate a reasonable set of statutory reforms that are not "amnesty" and don’t involve a "path to citizenship."

But as President Trump has noted on a few occasions, he doesn’t have to wait on them, as he has the "very powerful power of the pardon," which is indeed complete and within his sole control.

He could use the power of pardon on any segment of the illegal immigrant population before COB today or on Thanksgiving if he wanted to.

What might a presidential pardon look like that would (1) reflect the views of a supermajority of Americans and (2) not create an incentive for immigrants to think they should come toward our country or overstay visas?

A number of violations of federal statutes could be the subject of a presidential pardon. Illegal entry into the country is a crime, as is an illegal return after deportation. It is also a civil offense—still within the pardon power—to have entered legally but to have overstayed the permitted time of presence in the country.

TRUMP'S IMMIGRATION OLIVE BRANCH THREATENS TO OPEN PANDORA'S BOX AS EXPERTS WARN OF FAR-REACHING FALLOUT

So ask the people around the table: What would you think of any sort of presidential pardon for those who have broken these laws? Is there a version of one you could endorse and even applaud?

President Jimmy Carter’s pardon of draft dodgers who had broken the Selective Service laws of the Vietnam era is a model and included this language:

"I, Jimmy Carter, President of the United States, do hereby grant a full, complete and unconditional pardon to: (1) all persons who may have committed any offense between August 4, 1964, and March 28, 1973, in violation of the Military Selective Service Act or any rule or regulation promulgated thereunder; and (2) all persons heretofore convicted, irrespective of the date of conviction, of any offense committed between August 4, 1964, and March 28, 1973, in violation of the Military Selective Service Act, or any rule or regulation promulgated thereunder, restoring to them full political, civil and other rights."

On its face, the pardon of 50 years ago was narrowly tailored, and its accompanying language specifically excluded those whose Selective Service violation involved force or violence and those who committed violations in connection with employment as an agent, officer, or employee of the Selective Service System.

It also did not cover military deserters or people who had gone AWOL from the armed forces.

TRUMP SAYS DEPORTATION PUSH HASN’T PUT 'SAME PRESSURE' ON FARMWORKERS, HOTEL STAFF: 'NOT EVEN CLOSE'

President Trump thus has it within his power to immediately and carefully address the excesses of deportation policy that he knows were "too tough."

Thus, President Trump is in a position to do a Nixon-to-China on illegal immigrants. There might be a "Trump-Schumer-Jeffries Regularization Act" a year down the road, a statute that should not include a general "amnesty" and cannot provide a "pathway to citizenship." Such a statute could provide a detailed legislative change to grant a right of continued residence to a defined subset of illegal immigrants upon a showing of certain conditions, such as no felony arrests, past or future, for people in the country for a decade or more.

But President Trump does not have to wait on Democrats, and indeed he shouldn’t, to make clear it was his decision. Pardon seekers would have to present proof of near-continuous employment and such other evidence of character and commitment as President Trump details in the language of the pardon. A pardon could be very focused and also include such conditions and exclusions as the president deems fit.

President Trump could issue such a pardon today. He can act tomorrow. He can act on Thanksgiving or Christmas. The pardon power is unlimited. If President Trump deploys it carefully, the public would first be thunderstruck and then almost wholly united in praising his act of mercy.

There is a very deep and broad sense of justice and fairness in the American public. The deportation of long-time residents who have worked hard and are raising families—especially those with children born in the country—deeply disturbs most Americans of all political persuasions. Continued deportation of individuals whose life circumstances jar ordinary voters especially upsets legal residents, family members, and friends of illegal immigrants.

Hardly a week goes by without a story of a deportation that elicits the pity of most Americans while triggering anger at government officials who are just applying the law. President Trump can unilaterally defuse the worst assaults on the collective American sense of justice. There will be critics, and they will be loud, but they would actually represent only a tiny portion of the country.

TRUMP BORDER CRACKDOWN DRIVES ENCOUNTERS TO RECORD OCTOBER LOW AS ZERO-RELEASE STREAK HITS 18 MONTHS, DHS SAYS

The deportation excesses of the past two years are also going to be a barrier to the return of Republican majorities in either the House or the Senate if they do not end. Reasonable people will disagree on the specifics of a presidential pardon (or of a statutory "regularization" bill down the road), but—assuming the Bell Curve applies to illegal immigrants—there are more than a million illegal immigrants who ought obviously to be deported as soon as possible and at least a million who are just as obviously good people and community members who should not be rousted out of their lives and deported.

The online world separates quickly from the reality of the American center on this issue, but President Trump intuits he has to course-correct on deportation policy. Thus, there is a great opportunity right now for a legacy achievement via his pardon power and down the road via statutory compromise, if Democrats do not overreach and seek political advantage from a "regularization" bill.

Presidents Obama and Biden could not bring themselves to do the necessary thing prior to such a statute, which was to have built the border wall.

President Trump has provided the necessary precondition to a wide-ranging pardon: He has shown that the border is secure. Now he can accomplish an immediate and vast good via the pardon power and begin negotiations on a breakthrough, provided the Democrats do not allow their extremists to poison the political well, even as center-right to conservative Republicans reject the instant denunciation of a pardon and every bill as "amnesty," which regularization efforts would not be.

The question for the adults at the Thanksgiving table on Thursday: If President Trump were to issue a pardon, to whom should it apply and what limits on that pardon should there be?

If I were White House Counsel Will Scharf, I would urge President Trump to begin with a fairly narrow pardon and one with explicit parameters that excluded felons and people who have been arrested for violent crimes. It should—at least in the first round—require those seeking its benefit to be able to show unbroken residence in the country prior to, say, January 21, 2020. It might also require proof of having worked and paid taxes and perhaps be limited to adults with children who are American citizens. There are a lot of fine points and exclusions to be debated here. The White House Counsel and his team could prepare many pardon options, and President Trump could decide among them.

TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY

The debate in the comments below or on a related Reddit forum will be angry but unrepresentative of the whole of the public, and President Trump already knows he must course-correct. If a pardon from President Trump does issue, it ought then to be the subject of careful consideration by serious people of goodwill, and their reactions should be guided by reason.

A carefully crafted pardon would be life-changing for more than a million people who would thereafter brook no criticism of Trump. It would lift an enormous burden from intact families of law-abiding people who work hard and have no inclination to break the law and who have had children in this country who are citizens. It should be easy to understand and to apply in practice. Its successful implementation could yield permission to remain in the country contingent on not committing a serious offense.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Such a pardon would immediately refocus the debate around deportation away from the deportation cases that trouble three-quarters or more of Americans. If you pay attention to these stories, you know there are many, many cases that jar ordinary Americans.

"Maybe we could touch the subject of immigration," said President Trump.

He is right to make that touch. If he did so with a pardon that was satisfactory to the vast majority of Americans, that touch would indeed be a golden one.

item.title: Commanders' Jayden Daniels spoils Joe Burrow's night, leads team to game-winning drive vs Bengals
item.description: Jayden Daniels' game-winning drive stunned Joe Burrow and the Cincinnati Bengals, 20-19, on "Monday Night Football" as Drew Stevens drilled the winner.
item.content:encoded:
Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow, the MVP frontrunner, was heading into another Primetime slate on "Monday Night Football" with NFL history on the line, as he could’ve been the first player ever to tally four or more touchdown passes in six straight games.

Well, he didn’t accomplish that, but against the 31st-ranked pass defense in the NFL, surely he was able to lead the Bengals past the Commanders, right?

Well, he seemed to do so with a strong, "Thank you!" to kicker Evan McPherson for drilling a 56-yard field goal with 46 seconds left through the wind.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

That is until Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels spoiled an 8-2 start for the Bengals through 10 games with a gutsy game-winning drive of his own to upset Cincinnati, 20-19, at Northwest Stadium on Monday night.

Daniels led the Commanders on five straight scoring drives before the Bengals retook their lead late in the fourth quarter, but they weren’t for six points. Rookie kicker Drew Stevens was called upon for all of them, but he kept the Commanders in the game by doing his job and knocking through three points each time.

On the final drive, Daniels needed to get Stevens into range to make it a perfect five for five, which would win Washington the game. The problem is Daniels had no timeouts left, making things a bit tricky.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

However, Antonio Williams, the third-round pick out of Clemson who had a fantastic night, came through in the most clutch way for Daniels when he hauled in a 22-yard strike to quickly get the ball to midfield. Then, after spiking the rock, Daniels linked up with Williams again, this time for 42 yards, giving Stevens a 26-yard field goal for the win.

He drilled it, and the Commanders and their fan base at home went ballistic as, for the second straight week, they came away with a miraculous victory to keep their NFC East division title hopes alive at 4-5-1. The New York Giants, whom the Commanders shocked on the road in a "Thursday Night Football" thriller last week, sit in first place at 6-3-1, but the Commanders have the tiebreaker over them now due to the win in Week 10.

Burrow and the Bengals couldn’t believe it, but this game certainly wasn’t what their offense has been doing of late.

The first half pouring rain didn’t help matters, but both defenses were suffocating the quarterbacks on the gridiron. Burrow and Daniels couldn’t get anything going, that is until the rain started to lighten up before the first half came to a close.

Burrow finally found the end zone when he dropped in another perfect ball this season to Tee Higgins. How in the world Higgins came down with the touchdown grab, as the ball wasn’t fully secured in one of his hands, was a feat.

However, Jacksonville Jaguars fans won’t be happy as it was eerily similar to Parker Washington’s no-touchdown call on Sunday against the New York Giants. This time, referees confirmed Higgins was in bounds and had control for the first touchdown of the game.

Daniels, though, made things very interesting for the second half when he ripped off a 47-yard run to get into the red zone for the first time. A few plays later, Jacory Croskey-Merritt, playing his first game since suffering a groin injury against the Giants in Week 5’s tie at home, scored to make it a 10-7 game.

Burrow was able to find Colbie Young in the third quarter for his first career touchdown, giving the Bengals a 17-10 lead. But back-to-back punts, while the Commanders continued to tack on points, made things tight down the stretch.

Cincinnati looked like they escaped with a win, but Washington continues to show the NFL that, until the clock hits zero, it’s simply not over.

Just like their playoff hopes.

item.title: Stadium lights go out during Bengals-Commanders game because vendor forgot about Monday Night Football
item.description: A power outage darkened Northwest Stadium with 11:59 left in the third quarter as Jayden Daniels and the Commanders faced Joe Burrow's Bengals.
item.content:encoded:
Play during Monday night's NFL game between the Cincinnati Bengals and Washington Commanders stopped briefly after the field lights went out.

The blackout happened with 11:59 left in the third quarter, early in Washington's first drive of the second half. 

Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels and wide receiver Stefon Diggs were lined up on third down when the stadium suddenly went dark. 

While the main overhead lights shut off, the smaller signs and video boards around the stands stayed lit.

On the ESPN broadcast, announcer Joe Buck told viewers that the stadium's lighting vendor never disabled its regular scheduled maintenance for 10 p.m. (ET) after forgetting there was a Monday night game. 

The lights came back on within moments, prompting Buck to say, "Let there be light," as referees restarted the game after a short wait.

The timing coincided with Washington's promoted fan blackout night, with the team wearing all-black uniforms.

The interruption did not slow down Washington's drive against Cincinnati quarterback Joe Burrow and the 7-2 Bengals, who entered the night on a five-game winning streak.

Trailing 10-7 at halftime after a 1-yard touchdown run by Washington running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt, the Commanders moved down the field once power returned and kicked a 36-yard field goal to tie the score at 10-10.

FSU-SMU GAME TURNS INTO OLD-SCHOOL FOOTBALL AFTER STADIUM POWER OUTAGE WIPES OUT IN-GAME COMMUNICATION

The brief delay marked the second time this month that a Bengals game was interrupted by stadium lights going out.

Earlier in November, Cincinnati's game against the Atlanta Falcons in Madrid was also interrupted by a fourth-quarter power outage.

item.title: Coast Guard boards 2 foreign ships bound for US amid reports of Iranian hacking probe
item.description: U.S. Coast Guard cyber teams boarded two foreign vessels in the Gulf of America after their networks were compromised by foreign cyber actors at sea.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Coast Guard deployed specialized cyber teams to board two foreign-flagged commercial ships bound for U.S. ports in August after indications that their networks had been compromised by "foreign cyber actors," a Coast Guard spokesperson told Fox News Digital on Monday.

The offshore operations took place Aug. 21 and 24 in the Gulf of America, with teams mitigating the threats before the vessels reached U.S. ports.

The confirmation came as The Wall Street Journal also reported Monday that U.S. authorities are investigating whether Iran was involved in dozens of cyberattacks targeting energy tankers.

FEARS OF CHINA SPYING ON US MILITARY PROMPT GOP HAWKS TO DEMAND RETALIATION AGAINST THE SHIPPING GIANT

"The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG), in close coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and federal cybersecurity experts, recently conducted joint offshore security boardings of two inbound foreign-flagged commercial vessels in the Gulf of America," a Coast Guard spokesperson said.

"The measures were designed to ensure the integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised by foreign cyber actors."

The Coast Guard said a specialized team of law enforcement personnel, Coast Guard Cyber Protection Team members, a vessel inspector and FBI Cyber Action Team operators boarded the first vessel Aug. 21 to investigate the suspected cybersecurity breach.

"The captain, crew, and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," the spokesperson added.

A similar multiagency boarding and safety verification operation was conducted Aug. 24 aboard the second vessel, also in the Gulf of America, the Coast Guard said.

FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE

No operational disruptions, vessel instability, threats to crew safety or environmental impacts have been reported.

The Coast Guard said it is coordinating with port operators, vessel owners and local maritime stakeholders to ensure port operations continue safely and without interruption.

According to The Wall Street Journal, attackers exploited vulnerabilities in Fortinet networking equipment, prompting Coast Guard boardings after crews received bomb threats warning that "traitor ships will burn in hell."

STRAIT OF HORMUZ CRISIS TRAPS 6,000 SAILORS AS ATTACKS ON SHIPS MOUNT, UN MARITIME CHIEF SAYS

As many as 50 vessels carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemicals and other potentially explosive cargo are believed to have been targeted, the outlet reported, citing U.S. officials.

A European shipping executive also said officers received threats on their cellphones.

A ransom letter addressed to the captain of the Liberian-flagged supertanker Prosperity, which was carrying about 2.3 million barrels of oil, described the operation as a "planned execution."

Hackers reportedly breached one vessel's propulsion and navigation systems, disrupting communications for about 30 hours and forcing the crew to switch to manual procedures, potentially delaying energy shipments to Asia and Europe.

AMERICA MUST DEFEND OUR DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE, HERE AND OVERSEAS, TO WIN THE NEXT WAR

"The Marine Transportation System is vital to America's economic prosperity and national security, and safeguarding it against potential cyber risks is a standard part of the United States Coast Guard's safety and security mission," the Coast Guard spokesperson said.

"Just as we monitor for mechanical or weather-related hazards, we incorporate cyber risk management into our routine, professional approach to facilitating commerce and ensuring safe vessel transits into and from our ports and waterways.

"While confirmed cyber disruptions in the maritime domain remain uncommon, even isolated technical issues can cause avoidable commercial delays.

"We encourage all maritime stakeholders to leverage Coast Guard Cyber Command’s free, non-regulatory technical resources to maintain strong digital hygiene and report any suspected anomalies to the National Response Center," the spokesperson added.

item.title: Newly elected Florida commissioner's son shot dead inside tent during camping trip
item.description: Local law enforcement is appealing for tips after a weekend camping trip along the Blackwater River ended in tragedy for a Florida official's family.
item.content:encoded:
A newly elected Florida politician is mourning the death of his son after the young man was fatally shot inside his tent during a weekend camping trip, his father confirmed Monday.

Joe Vinson, who made history earlier this year as the first non-party-affiliated county commissioner elected in Escambia County, announced the tragedy on Instagram, revealing that his son, Carey Washington Vinson, was killed while camping with friends near the Blackwater River in the Florida Panhandle.

"I don’t know how to say this," Joe Vinson wrote. "Our son Carey Washington Vinson is dead. He was camping with friends on the Blackwater River last night when a gunshot from outside their campsite struck him in his tent."

CALIFORNIA NURSING STUDENT AND MOM ARRESTED MONTHS AFTER MAN’S BODY TURNS UP IN RAVINE: POLICE

He added, "It’s an ongoing investigation, and I don’t have any more details at this time. We are shocked and heartbroken about our sweet boy."

According to the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office, officers were dispatched to the Blackwater River area on Sunday following a 911 call about a shooting.

First responders arrived to find a male victim with a gunshot wound to the head and pronounced him dead at the scene.

RUSH HOUR ROAD RAGE SUSPECT’S BAIL REVOKED AS SLAIN UTILITY WORKER’S SUPPORTERS SHOUT AT ACCUSED MURDERER

Carey, 19, and his friends had been camping on sandbars along the river since Friday, Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office Chief Deputy Randy Tifft told People Magazine. 

Law enforcement has not yet said whether they believe the shooting was intentional or accidental.

Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons offered condolences to the commissioner's family on Facebook.

"There are simply no words that can ease the pain of losing a child," Simmons said. "I ask that you join me in keeping Joe and his entire family in your thoughts and prayers during this incredibly difficult time. May God grant them strength, comfort, and peace in the days ahead."

LOUISIANA MAN ACCUSED OF RANDOM NATURE TRAIL MURDER, KILLING COWORKER WITH CROSSBOW DAYS LATER

Detectives are urging anyone who was in the area or witnessed suspicious activity to come forward.

"This incident remains under active investigation," a spokesperson for the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office told Fox News Digital in an email. "We will provide updates as additional information becomes available for release."

item.title: Army sergeant pleads guilty to cashing in on US military secrets in China-linked plot, DOJ says
item.description: Sgt. Jian Zhao faces up to 10 years in prison after pleading guilty to selling national defense information from Joint Base Lewis-McChord, prosecutors say.
item.content:encoded:
An active-duty U.S. Army sergeant pleaded guilty Monday in a yearslong plot that turned his access to sensitive military information into a payday from buyers in China.

Jian Zhao, 37, used his personal cellphone to photograph restricted Army documents, handed over excerpts from technical manuals for the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, or HIMARS, and put military computers and government hard drives up for sale, federal prosecutors said.

"Protecting our national security depends on holding accountable those who compromise their oath and endanger the security of our armed forces," U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford wrote on X.

CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN

"Jian Zhao violated that trust by exploiting his access to military information and equipment for personal profit while knowingly providing materials to individuals linked to China."

Zhao pleaded guilty to conspiring to gather, transmit and transfer national defense information. Prosecutors said he enlisted in 2017 and served as a battery supply sergeant at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington, where his duties and security clearance gave him access to sensitive Army information and equipment.

CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN

The documents Zhao photographed covered Army operations, communications networks, military exercises and rocket and missile systems, prosecutors said.

He also took military storage devices without permission and collected thousands of dollars for materials he described as sensitive, secret or top secret.

SENIOR US ARMY SOLDIER ARRESTED IN UK ON SUSPICION OF SPYING FOR RUSSIA

"This guilty plea reflects a deliberate betrayal of the oath every Soldier takes to defend our nation and safeguard our fellow service members," said Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, who leads Army Counterintelligence Command.

Stinchon said the scheme put soldiers at risk and urged troops to report suspicious activity or outreach.

CALIFORNIA REALTOR NABBED AT LAX IN ALLEGED CHINA SPY CASE TARGETING TAIWAN PRESIDENT’S RELATIVE

Prosecutors traced the plot back to late 2021. Ruoyu Duan, a former Army soldier living in Hillsboro, Oregon, recruited Zhao and other active-duty troops to provide defense information and helped arrange payments from buyers in China, prosecutors said. Duan previously pleaded guilty to conspiring to transmit national defense information.

Federal agents arrested Zhao at his home in Lacey, Washington, on March 6, 2025, and recovered about $30,000 in cash, electronic devices and multiple Army hard drives.

FORMER CALIFORNIA MAYOR ADMITS TO SECRETLY WORKING FOR CHINA, SPREADING BEIJING PROPAGANDA IN US

Under his plea agreement, Zhao agreed to forfeit $17,500 in proceeds from the scheme and give up his claim to the seized cash.

"By pleading guilty, Jian Zhao has admitted to betraying that trust and abusing the responsibilities that came with his position and security clearance," said Doug Olson, the FBI’s special agent in charge in Portland.

"Those who choose to compromise sensitive military information for personal gain put our nation's interests at risk, and the FBI, alongside our law enforcement and military partners, remains committed to holding them accountable," he continued.

Zhao faces up to 10 years in federal prison, a $250,000 fine and up to three years of supervised release. His sentencing is set for March 1, 2027.

item.title: Once again, the College Football Playoff selection committee has an opportunity to fix their mistakes
item.description: The College Football Playoff committee faces scrutiny as Alabama's best wins once again lost this weekend while Indiana dropped five spots for the same reason.
item.content:encoded:
Well, we're back for another week.

Tuesday evening, the College Football Playoff selection committee will release their latest top-25 poll, despite our best efforts, and ESPN will host Committee Chair Hunter Yurachek for a post-release interview. And already, they've trotted out Heather Dinich to justify whatever absurdities they have coming for us.

But before going into what we can expect, it's worth quickly revisiting how we got here.

WILL THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF SELECTION COMMITTEE EMBARRASS ITSELF AGAIN WITH NEW RANKINGS?

In week one, the committee's poll consistently overrated SEC teams, with virtually all of them sitting several spots, at least, ahead of where more unbiased, objective metrics-based system placed them. That unsurprising trend continued in week two, and despite the outrage and complaints from fans and analysts about week one's poll, the committee doubled and tripled down.

The Indiana Hoosiers dropped five spots, despite sitting out with a bye, and Yurachek's explanation for it was disastrous at best, and disqualifying and insulting at worst.

"Every team that Indiana had played to date in the Big Ten all lost and that affected their strength of schedule rank and the committee's review of Indiana," he said. "The quarterback play in general and the offensive play in general is kind of a discussion point of Indiana ... They've won games because of their defense and not their offense."

Ignoring everything else, the important note was that Indiana's Big Ten opponents all lost in the same week, hurting their strength of schedule. Then, between week two and week three, the exact same thing happened to the Alabama Crimson Tide. South Carolina lost to an awful Arkansas team by 28 points. Texas A&M lost at home, again. Mississippi State lost its fifth game in a row with yet another defensive disaster class. Kentucky lost its second in a row, as its offense continued to struggle, then LSU lost at home again too.

Yurachek and the committee didn't drop the Tide a single spot. Then when asked about it, gave a thoroughly discrediting answer.

"Alabama faced a similar circumstance where five of their SEC opponents all lost, but it didn't have the same impact on their strength of schedule that it had on Indiana's strength of schedule," he said. "Actually, it is very minimal for Alabama because of the quality and the strength of schedule of those five teams that lost."

There are only a few certainties in life, death, taxes, and the selection committee worshipping at the feet of the Crimson Tide.

The good news for fans who want to see some objectivity? The committee has another opportunity this week, thanks to another rough Saturday for the Tide's strength of schedule, to show that they're willing to be unbiased and not play favorites.

Again, the stated justification for Indiana dropping five spots was that all the Big Ten teams they played lost in the same week. When that exact scenario played out for Alabama, they did not drop at all. This weekend? It got worse.

The Tide's "signature" win thus far was the Kentucky Wildcats. In conference, they also beat LSU, Texas A&M, Vanderbilt, Mississippi State without Kamario Taylor, and South Carolina. Out of conference, they beat Florida State, East Carolina, and Chattanooga.

Here's how their primary wins did this past weekend:

HERE'S HOW BAD THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF'S SELECTION COMMITTEE RANKINGS ACTUALLY ARE

Every single team that provided a "big" win for Alabama and played a competitive program lost. Kentucky's fallen off a cliff, losing three straight games and scoring just 34 combined points. South Carolina showed why their ranking was always based on unjustified assumptions of SEC strength. Vanderbilt and Texas A&M continued to be two of the worst Power 4 teams in the country, LSU was LSU, and Tennessee Tech provided the free SEC November bye week, allowing the Bulldogs to end their five-game losing streak.

With these results, here are the records of Alabama's signature wins this year:

The combined records of those teams, including FCS wins, is just 37-40. Meanwhile, Alabama lost to the only two elite teams they played, Georgia and Tennessee.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Is that enough? Is that finally enough for the committee to admit they might have made a mistake by assuming that every SEC team deserved to be ranked because they're in the SEC? And that in doing so, they provide undeserved strength of schedule boosts to teams like Alabama? Do they acknowledge that basing their discussions on "ranked wins" is insane, considering how flawed their rankings are? Or that margin of victory in the SEC is a nonsensical "standard" that begs the question?

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

None of this is to pick on Alabama. The Tide aren't doing this themselves, they're a very good team that at this point clearly deserves a spot in the CFB Playoff. The issue is that their treatment by the committee exemplifies the ridiculous double standards being employed here, in order to engineer their preferred outcomes.

One of the most aggrieved parties is Tennessee, who beat the Tide on the field, has a similar resume and identical win-loss record, yet sits well behind the Tide.

Funnily enough, with all the hand-wringing over Indiana's supposedly "easy" schedule, per ESPN's SP+ metric, which has a "strength of schedule" and "strength of resume" component, Indiana's slate is the 38th toughest in the country? The Georgia Bulldogs? Just 44th. USC's played a harder schedule than Tennessee, yet is buried with little hope of reaching the playoff, even should they beat a top-10 UCLA team on Saturday.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Then there's Wake Forest, who have obliterated most of the teams on their 56th ranked schedule. Their "resume SP+" ranking is No. 5. They won't be anywhere close to that in Tuesday's poll, because they have the wrong brand name and conference affiliation patch.

The committee has an opportunity, now more than ever, to show that they can and will be fair, objective, interested in growing, and committed to evaluating metrics that matter, not ludicrous "margins in SEC games" idiocy. Will they take it? Well, we'll find out, but based on their track record, it's a near-certainty the answer will be a resounding no.

item.title: James Carville warns Gavin Newsom faces California baggage in potential 2028 run
item.description: Democratic strategist James Carville says Gavin Newsom faces a major 2028 hurdle in that voters are weary of "California" style coastal politics.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic strategist James Carville suggested that California Gov. Gavin Newsom will have to reckon with Americans weary of liberal coastal politics if he runs in 2028.

Speaking on the Politicon podcast with political adviser Mark McKinnon Friday, Carville weighed in on potential contenders for the 2028 Democratic nomination. When asked about Newsom’s chances, he argued that one key issue stands in his way.

"Well, his strength is he runs the biggest state. He's got a huge fundraising base. There's no doubt about it. If you’re the governor of California, you could raise a lot of money," Carville said. "His problem is, ‘Are we going to do this California sh-- again? Really? Is that what we're going to do?’"

"He's got to overcome that kind of barrier," Carville warned, suggesting many voters are wary of an "uber coastal candidate" leading the country.

NEWSOM ROASTED ONLINE FOR 'STAGED' FLY-FISHING INTERVIEW WITH CNN ANCHOR WHERE HE DROPPED MAJOR 2028 HINT

McKinnon said he was initially skeptical that Newsom might be "a little too slick, a little too Hollywood," but was impressed after interviewing him several times on his own podcast.

"I mean, he's got chops," McKinnon said.

Carville agreed that Newsom is quick on his feet and possesses real political skill, noting that navigating California's Democratic politics is far more difficult than outsiders assume. He also credited Newsom for being authentic to his roots, comparing the governor's California persona to his own Louisiana identity.

NEWSOM ADMITS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST IDEAS ‘MAINSTREAM’ IN DEMOCRAT PARTY: ‘PRETTY ALIGNED’

"To his credit, he's a real California guy," he said. "He don't try to fake it."

Other party insiders remain skeptical of Newsom's national appeal.

Veteran Democratic strategist Doug Schoen suggested that "Gavin Newsom has no clear identity. Some days he's a moderate Bill Clinton type and on other days he tries to be a progressive — for example, he's for a national wealth tax, and he has recently commuted the sentences of hundreds of death row inmates."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"His strengths are that he's telegenic, quick on his feet and engaging," Schoen added. "His weaknesses are that he has no clear message or strategy, and that he goes whichever way the wind blows."

Still, Schoen acknowledged Newsom is a serious contender because of his fundraising power and home-state base. Although Newsom has previously said he would not run if former Vice President Kamala Harris enters the race, Schoen said the governor appears eager to launch a campaign of his own.

"This seems like a warning shot towards Kamala, as there is every indication that he's chomping at the bit to run himself."

item.title: Bengals wide receiver Tee Higgins skips designer labels to pay tribute to Fiona the Hippo
item.description: Tee Higgins skipped loud designer fits for a Fiona the Hippo shirt before the Bengals faced the Washington Commanders, a tribute the whole city felt.
item.content:encoded:
NFL pregame arrivals have turned into a weekly contest to see who can wear the loudest designer clothes, which is why Tee Higgins rolling into the stadium in a Fiona shirt as a meaningful tribute hit so differently.

Before the Cincinnati Bengals kicked off against the Washington Commanders, Higgins walked into the stadium rocking the shirt, instantly connecting with a city still bummed out over a rough week.

The Cincinnati Zoo announced on Nov. 19 that the nine-year-old hippo had died, and the news hit the region hard.

Folks across Southwest Ohio treated Fiona like a hometown icon, and she was a massive part of everyday life in Cincinnati.

DEION SANDERS TO THE NFL? CRAIG CARTON EXPLAINS WHY HE CAN SAVE A FLOUNDERING NFL FRANCHISE?

Born six weeks premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017, she weighed just 29 pounds and faced long odds of surviving. Keepers bottle-fed her around the clock until she pulled through, and over the next nine years she turned into a Cincinnati staple.

Her face popped up on downtown murals and on everything from local beer cans to signs.

Earlier in the month, a visitor's knit hat bounced off a ceiling fan into her habitat, and Fiona swallowed it.

ZOO SHARES NECROPSY FINDINGS FOLLOWING FIONA THE HIPPO’S HEARTBREAKING DEATH

Zoo vets spent days trying to help her recover, though she passed away, leaving heartbroken fans to stack flowers and notes outside the zoo gates all weekend.

Most guys in the league spend all week coordinating designer outfits for the cameras, yet Higgins rolled in wearing a local zoo tribute every family in Southwest Ohio immediately recognized.

item.title: Four illegal immigrants among six arrested in Florida slaughterhouse torture case, AG says
item.description: Six workers at Ali Meat International, an Orlando halal slaughterhouse, face animal cruelty charges as four are held on ICE detainers, officials say.
item.content:encoded:
Customers could buy an animal and slaughter it themselves at a public event in Orlando, where video of what happened next led to six arrests and drew a rebuke from Florida’s attorney general, who called it "pure evil."

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday that six workers at Ali Meat International, a halal slaughterhouse, face charges in the case. In a post on X, he singled out four workers he said were in the country illegally.

"Florida will not tolerate the abuse and torture of defenseless animals," Uthmeier wrote. "Four are illegal aliens who never should have been here, and they will be punished and sent back to where they came from."

ICE-LED FLORIDA OPERATION NETS 500 — INCLUDING ILLEGAL ALIENS ACCUSED OF MURDER, CHILD ABUSE, CARTEL TIES

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement placed detainers on those four workers, according to Uthmeier’s office. At Monday’s press conference, Uthmeier said the state would prosecute them before any deportations.

State agricultural agents arrested the six workers Friday while serving a warrant at the business. Among them was manager Nadeem Shakeel, 44, who faces up to 105 years in prison if convicted as charged, according to the attorney general’s office.

WOMAN PLEADS GUILTY TO PAYING FOR SEXUAL TORTURE VIDEOS INVOLVING MONKEYS FOR ONLINE GROUP: 'SICK PERSON'

U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said federal food safety investigators reviewed video from the facility and found violations of federal humane slaughter law. She said USDA immediately revoked the facility’s permission to slaughter livestock without federal inspectors present.

Rollins said USDA’s Office of Inspector General joined Florida authorities in Friday’s operation and that she was in Orlando to thank investigators.

WARNING: GRAPHIC DETAILS

"Animal cruelty is unacceptable," Rollins wrote. "We will hold those responsible accountable."

The state opened its investigation in August 2025 after a person who saw the June event advertised on social media turned over 19 videos. In one recording, investigators say, a worker put a knife in the hand of a boy believed to be 12 or 13, then held his wrist to make him cut a sheep’s throat.

"Subjecting children firsthand to this horrific behavior is unthinkable," Uthmeier said at the press conference.

CALIFORNIA TEEN FACES PRISON AFTER VIRAL VIDEO SHOWS HIM SQUARING UP, REPEATEDLY KICKING SEA LION IN THE FACE

Investigators said the videos showed workers carrying 16 lambs upside down by their legs, cutting their throats and tossing them into a pile. An employee walked over the lambs while several were still moving, according to Uthmeier’s office.

Investigators also said cattle were repeatedly shocked with electric prods, including in the mouth and face, and that one customer made at least 15 cuts as an animal struggled to breathe.

69 LIVE ANIMALS FOUND STUFFED IN PILLOWCASES IN HIDDEN CAR COMPARTMENT AFTER BORDER ARREST: FEDS

Assistant Statewide Prosecutor Lauryn Day said complaints about the business dated back to 2021. During Friday’s search, she said, investigators found live animals standing in mud and feces and storage areas littered with dirty socks and trash. The animals were placed in temporary care while the state works with the U.S. Department of Agriculture to arrange their transfer.

"Religious beliefs do not provide a license to disregard animal welfare laws or subject animals to unnecessary suffering," Day said.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson said his department was investigating other animal cruelty cases and urged anyone who knows about similar practices to come forward. "We’re not going to tolerate animal cruelty here in the state of Florida," he said.

Shakeel told investigators he organized the event, oversaw staff and customers and handled the money, according to Uthmeier’s office. Agents said they found a stolen rifle in the office that Shakeel acknowledged was his. He faces a firearm theft charge in addition to animal cruelty, cattle abuse and conspiracy charges.

Another worker, Gelacio Santiz, told investigators he began slaughtering animals while they were still conscious, the office said.

The attorney general’s office identified the four workers with ICE detainers. Gelacio Santiz, 36, and Lorenzo Santis Diaz, 26, are from Mexico. Muhammad Irfan Khan, 44, is from Pakistan, and Jean Deolis, 57, is from Haiti.

VIDEO SHOWS FLORIDA FOOD TRUCK WORKERS FLEEING FROM ICE DURING TALLAHASSEE IMMIGRATION RAID

Belal Khaled Dohast, 45, was also arrested and faces animal cruelty and conspiracy charges.

All six were being held at the Orange County Jail as of Monday’s announcement. Day said each had made an initial court appearance and that their bond conditions bar them from contacting one another, having contact with animals or returning to the business.

Uthmeier said the slaughterhouse was no longer operating as of Monday and that the state was considering civil action. His office said the criminal investigation remains open and more charges are expected.

item.title: SEC threatens the nuclear option as LSU’s rebellion puts conference future at risk, RJ Luis plans to sue
item.description: The SEC filed a motion signaling a special meeting to decide on terminating LSU after Will Wade played RJ Luis despite telling Greg Sankey he wouldn't.
item.content:encoded:
UPDATE: On Monday night, RJ Luis' attorney reportedly said that the basketball player would be suing the SEC and commissioner Greg Sankey for damages related to the conference violating a judge's order that led to LSU no longer rostering his client. 

In addition, Clayton made it very clear that he is looking to get SEC Presidents on the record through depositions on whether they were acting in collusion with Greg Sankey to undermine RJ's attempt at playing basketball this season. This, along with others, is a reason why the SEC has such a problem with how LSU has conducted themselves, even if they were not directly tied to the situation. 

The SEC’s ongoing feud with LSU now comes with a threat that would have once seemed unthinkable: kicking the Tigers out of the conference in a meeting Dec. 3.

In a federal court filing Monday, the Southeastern Conference said it will hold a special meeting next month to consider whether to "terminate" LSU’s membership amid the ongoing fight involving RJ Luis and two football players.

Whether conference leaders would actually take that step is another question. But after months of legal threats, courtroom showdowns and last-minute roster decisions, the SEC is putting LSU’s future on the table.

LANE KIFFIN’S ROSTER FIGHT SET THE STAGE, WILL WADE JUST THREW A GRENADE IN LSU-SEC WAR WITH RJ LUIS

The latest escalation follows Will Wade’s decision to play Luis against Louisiana-Monroe last week, six days after a Baton Rouge judge granted the former professional basketball player an injunction allowing him to compete.

That appearance reignited a fight that began months earlier, when Lane Kiffin’s football program considered rostering two players with NFL experience in the preseason.

On the eve of LSU’s season opener against Clemson, school officials ultimately decided against adding Dae’Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris to the roster, despite a judge’s order permitting them to play.

By then, the dispute had already spilled into federal court.

The day before that roster decision, SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey testified in the football players’ eligibility lawsuit against the conference and NCAA. That same day, the SEC filed a federal lawsuit against LSU President Wade Rousse and other university officials, including Kiffin.

DEION SANDERS TO THE NFL? CRAIG CARTON EXPLAINS WHY HE CAN SAVE A FLOUNDERING NFL FRANCHISE?

The conference argued that using a court order to circumvent its eligibility rules interfered with its First Amendment right to govern its membership.

LSU has since asked a federal judge to dismiss the lawsuit. While both sides await a ruling, the SEC’s latest filing adds another layer to a fight that keeps finding ways to get uglier.

The possibility that LSU would roster Luis was always going to create another confrontation.

This is the same school that kept the SEC guessing about Wright and Harris until the final hours before football rosters were due. When Luis added the conference to his eligibility lawsuit last month, another showdown seemed inevitable.

LSU LEAVES FORMER PRO-ATHLETES OFF FINAL ROSTER, ONE NIGHT BEFORE SEC TAKES LANE KIFFIN AND TIGERS TO COURT

Even though a judge granted Luis an injunction to play, there was an expectation within the SEC president's circle that the Tigers would not actually put him on the court.

To make matters worse, one of the attorneys representing RJ Luis, Tony Clayton, filed a motion to hold Greg Sankey in contempt of court on the same day.

SEC ACCUSES LSU OF DEFYING ITS RULES AS WILL WADE’S BASKETBALL ROSTER ADDS FUEL TO A BURNING FIRE

According to Greg Sankey, that expectation came from assurances by Wade and LSU athletic director Verge Ausberry.

"Before Defendants rostered Mr. Luis on Nov. 17, 2026, as discussed below, LSU officials indicated to me on multiple occasions—including a text message from Defendant Ausberry to me on September 5, 2026 and a phone call between Defendant Wade and me on October 14, 2026 — that Mr. Luis would not play for LSU’s basketball team," Sankey said on Monday in a declaration filed in federal court.

LSU PRESIDENT WADE ROUSSE ENDS LANE KIFFIN’S SEC SHOWDOWN, BUT THERE IS STILL RELATIONSHIPS TO MEND

Then Wade sent RJ Luis into the game last Wednesday, and whatever understanding existed between LSU and the conference went out the window.

It was the following day, according to multiple sources, that LSU President Wade Rousse took a phone call from Sankey to let him know the seriousness of what had just transpired the previous night and that SEC presidents were preparing to discuss how to penalize the Tigers on teleconference taking place later that afternoon.

That evening, Rousse released a statement announcing that he had instructed Wade to stop playing Luis.

While that might have calmed the waters for about 20 minutes, SEC presidents were furious that LSU would once again put them in a position to potentially act.

The prospect still seems unlikely. Expelling LSU would require a two-thirds vote (11), and scheduling a meeting to consider that option does not mean the votes are there, yet.

But dismissing this as another empty threat would ignore how far the dispute has escalated.

After LSU and Will Wade pulled the pin and throwing the grenade last week by playing RJ Luis, the conference is now prepared to discuss the matter further.

INSIDE A LOUISIANA COURTROOM: SEC-LSU LEGAL CIRCUS PLAYED OUT LIKE A JOHN GRISHAM NOVEL IN STUNNING SHOWDOWN

Also, none of the shenanigans involving LSU over the past four months happened without President Wade Rousse, and even Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry, giving the athletic department permission to test the SEC's power.

"That was the final straw for SEC leaders, they were ready to penalize them (LSU) in some form or fashion," one source familiar with the discussions told OutKick last week. "You can only poke the bear so many times before they decide to pounce, and they (SEC Presidents and Chancellors) had seen enough nonsense from LSU.

"Who knows if they would have actually boycotted games, or even tried. But lawyers from schools within the conference were going through their options. This whole thing is just annoying. Like, get your s— together, and I mean everyone involved."

LSU’s repeated challenges to the conference have unfolded with the backing of Rousse and Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry. The school has shown a willingness to test how much authority the SEC can exercise when a judge has cleared an athlete to play.

That is the heart of this fight: LSU has leaned on court orders allowing athletes to compete, while the SEC has defended its right to enforce conference eligibility rules.

Playing Luis made clear that LSU was willing to push that conflict further, even with a federal lawsuit hanging over the dispute in an Alabama courtroom.

For now, the immediate question is how far SEC leaders are willing to go. What began as an eligibility dispute now carries consequences that reach well beyond a roster spot.

The SEC has put its most drastic option on the table. Next month, we find out whether conference leaders are prepared to act on it — or whether the threat itself is the point.

item.title: Unsealed warrant documents for Ilhan Omar's DC home raid reveal decades-long scope of investigation
item.description: The redacted search warrant for Homeland Security Investigations' raid on Ilhan Omar's Washington D.C. home was released, with phone and passport seized.
item.content:encoded:
Heavily redacted versions of documents used to justify a search warrant and raid on the Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., were released to the public Monday evening.

Despite the level of redaction, the documents provide more insight into the scope of the investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman. 

In an ex parte brief in support of an affidavit for a search warrant, federal prosecutors say they're searching for all "records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of [redacted], those violations involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present (the 'Target Offenses)."

While accounts vary, even from the congresswoman herself, Omar was born in 1981 or 1982. She does not have a birth certificate. She came to the United States in 1995 with her father. Fox News Digital confirmed just after the Oct. 12 raid of her home, that investigators were looking into alleged immigration fraud, potentially related to how Omar and her father filled out her immigration paperwork. 

In another document, arguing that the court mischaracterized the government's arguments in ex parte proceedings, prosecutors make it clear that the investigation into Omar spans decades. 

"The United States believes that ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades— beginning long before she was ever in Congress," the document says. 

Fox News Digital reached out to a spokesperson for Omar. 

In a rare move, Obama-appointed federal Judge James Boasberg ordered the documents' release last week, telling the Department of Justice (DOJ) to submit proposed redactions before the materials were made public on Monday. Judge Boasberg, in order dated October 9, 2026, agreed initially to seal the documents due to "such reasonable grounds to believe the disclosure will result in flight from prosecution, destruction of or tampering with evidence, intimidation of potential witnesses, and serious jeopardy to the investigation."

Search warrants typically remain sealed until there is an arrest in a criminal case.

Fifteen media outlets, led by The New York Times, along with watchdog group Judicial Watch, sued President Donald Trump's DOJ for the release of the documents used to conduct the raid of a sitting congresswoman's residence. The outlets claimed that viewing the documents was in the public interest, while the government attempted to block the release by arguing that it was a violation of investigative protocol.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE PAVES WAY TO UNSEAL ILHAN OMAR SEARCH WARRANT IN BLOW TO TRUMP'S DOJ

Omar's Washington, D.C., home was raided on Oct. 12, 2026 — an unprecedented action to take against a sitting lawmaker, especially when there is less than a month until the Election Day where they are seeking reelection. The raid did not impact Omar in winning a fifth term in the House of Representatives.

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the chief investigative body of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), conducted the raid last month. Omar's personal phone, computer and passport were seized as evidence in the search. Authorities are also in possession of her DNA. 

Additionally, the lawmaker's sister, Sahra Noor, voluntarily submitted to questions from investigators during the week of the raid. Investigators are probing whether Omar or her late father — or both — lied on her citizenship paperwork, sources told Fox News Digital.

In a motion seeking to prevent the federal search warrant for the raid from being unsealed, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia referred to Omar as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar." Sources later told Fox News Digital that Ilhan Omar is not the congresswoman's "real name."

REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES

That news caused speculation that Omar married her brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, to resurface. The pair married in 2009, and divorced in 2017.

Omar has not been charged with a crime and has repeatedly denied wrongdoing. She has characterized the investigation as politically motivated, saying President Donald Trump is targeting her.

"For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," her office said in a statement after the raid. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."

The Somali-born congresswoman came to the United States as a child in 1995, after decades of civil unrest in her home country. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, served as a colonel in the Somali National Army under the brutal Siad Barre regime.

Barre's regime systematically killed between 50,000 and 200,000 members of the Isaaq clan in what is known as the Isaaq genocide. He was deposed in 1991.

item.title: Ukraine’s drone strike on Russian warship in Libya risks ‘serious escalation,’ former official warns
item.description: Morgan Murphy warned the Ukrainian sea drone strike on the Russian corvette Mercury in Benghazi risks a serious escalation of the nearly five-year war.
item.content:encoded:
The Ukrainian sea drone strike that capsized and sank a Russian warship in Libya on Sunday risks a "serious escalation" of the nearly five-year war, a former U.S. national security adviser warned Monday, calling the operation a "giant tantrum" by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Morgan Murphy, a former press secretary to the secretary of defense, also told Fox News Digital that the nighttime attack on the Russian corvette Mercury in the Libyan port city of Benghazi could further strain relations between Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump, while echoing frustrations that he said also plagued former President Joe Biden's administration.

"The strike on the Russian corvette Mercury in North Africa — in Libya specifically — is a serious escalation of the war in Ukraine," Murphy claimed.

"Calling the Benghazi strike a giant tantrum could be one interpretation of it, and it's not unusual behavior for him," Murphy said of Zelenskyy.

RUSSIAN WARSHIP SINKS OFF LIBYA AS SUSPECTED UKRAINIAN STRIKES TAKE WAR BEYOND BLACK SEA

Murphy also argued that Zelenskyy's willingness to pursue military objectives that complicate Washington's diplomatic priorities has frustrated previous administrations.

"This is why I think the Biden administration was frustrated with Zelenskyy, and why the Trump administration has been frustrated with Zelenskyy: he's acting like an independent player and not an ally," Murphy said.

Biden had reportedly lost his temper during a June 2022 phone call after Zelenskyy requested additional military assistance shortly after the White House announced a $1 billion aid package for Ukraine.

In his recently released memoir, Biden also revealed private frustrations with Zelenskyy, describing the Ukrainian leader as moody, stubborn and less grateful than expected.

UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC

Murphy went on to suggest the Benghazi drone strike could also complicate Trump's efforts to broker an end to the war, particularly after the president met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a historic summit without Zelenskyy.

"The President just had a successful meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, and he met them without Zelenskyy present, as is the right of the President of the United States to meet with whom he likes when he pleases," Murphy said.

"Zelenskyy was clearly upset about that, and this attack is him showing the President of the United States that he's still very relevant."

The operation, coordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and armed forces, targeted the Russian vessel in port, raising questions about where the drones originated and whether the conflict could spread further beyond Ukraine's borders.

Zelenskyy praised the strike Monday in a post on X, calling it "An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war."

Murphy argued that the Ukrainian leader is increasingly under pressure to demonstrate Kyiv can still deliver significant military victories as Trump pursues a diplomatic resolution.

"What he's looking for here is, I believe, a victory, because Ukraine has found more aid and sympathy on the world stage when it's winning," Murphy said.

Ukraine initially drew widespread international support after resisting Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, defying expectations that Moscow would quickly overwhelm Kyiv.

"Ukraine performed much better against an enemy five times its size, and human nature loves an underdog."

"There was a deep outpouring of sympathy — and more importantly, support — for Ukraine after that initial flop of a Russian invasion," Murphy said.

UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

But as the conflict has dragged on, Murphy argued, Ukraine has struggled to sustain the enthusiasm that followed Russia's initial setbacks, with the fighting descending into what he described as a "stalemate and a war of attrition."

"Zelenskyy is having a harder time building support," he said of the current state of play.

"As he saw the President meet with Russia and meet with Xi Jinping in China, he needed a victory, and he needed a dramatic attack — so an asymmetric attack was on the board."

The Benghazi strike also underscores Ukraine's expanding ability to target Russian military assets thousands of miles from its territory, although questions remain about how the operation was carried out.

"Ukraine has taken credit for it, but they've been coy about where it was launched from," Murphy said.

"There's some speculation that it was launched from within Libya. Others say that it came from a mothership, which is totally plausible — that they took an innocuous-looking cargo ship and launched these drones out of it."

Murphy said the operation reflects a broader transformation in modern warfare, with military planners still grappling with the implications of increasingly sophisticated drone attacks.

"What we are watching unfold in real time is a total shift in the nature of warfare. It's really unheralded," he said.

UKRAINE’S DRONE REVOLUTION SHOWS RUSSIA IS DANGEROUSLY UNPREPARED. BUT, SO IS AMERICA

"It will take time — planners' time and nations' time — to understand how to react to this kind of aggression."

Beyond the military implications, Murphy warned that the strike could undermine diplomatic efforts in Washington to negotiate an end to the conflict.

"There is a very concerted group of diplomats and thought leaders in D.C. who want to see a diplomatic end to this conflict sooner rather than later," Murphy said.

"They see that as being in the best interest of the United States and the world, but most importantly, they see it in the best interest of the Ukrainian people."

Murphy said those pushing for a negotiated settlement would likely view the reported strike in Libya as a setback to Trump's peace efforts.

"A lot of thinkers in Washington want this to end, and they'll see this escalation in Libya as counterproductive to what the President is trying to do."

item.title: El-Sayed says he'll work with 'a--hole' Ted Cruz if he has to get things done
item.description: Sen. Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., called Ted Cruz "an a------" in an interview with the Wall Street Journal Sunday, but vowed to work with him in the Senate.
item.content:encoded:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., called Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, "an a--hole" in an interview with The Wall Street Journal Sunday despite saying that he plans to work with him in the future.

After El-Sayed's electoral victory earlier this month, Wall Street Journal reporter Sabrina Siddiqui noted the Michigan Democrat has furthered tension between both Republican and Democratic colleagues. Among them was Cruz, who previously called El-Sayed a "jihadist" based on reported ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.

"He's an a--hole," El-Sayed said. "But if he's the a--hole from Texas with whom I have to work, I'll work with the a--hole from Texas. I'll still call him an a--hole. But if we're going to get some things done, let's get some things done."

CRUZ SAYS THERE'S 'REAL RISK THAT AMERICANS WILL DIE' IF EL-SAYED GAINS ACCESS TO US INTELLIGENCE

Cruz told the WSJ that he would "work with anyone who's doing positive things for America," though he did not respond to El-Sayed's crude remarks.

Fox News Digital reached out to Cruz's office for comment.

El-Sayed has also fought with Democratic senators, particularly on the issue of U.S. support for Israel. During the election season, El-Sayed called for efforts to primary pro-Israel Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., referring to him as an "ogre on a pike" that could be used as a warning to moderate candidates.

EL-SAYED TELLS HEGSETH TO RESIGN AFTER IMPEACHMENT EFFORT FAILS: 'MAKE IT EASY FOR EVERYBODY'

He is also among a growing number of Democratic senators and senators-elect calling for Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to be replaced as the Democratic Senate leader in the incoming Congress.

Nevertheless, El-Sayed told WSJ that he was willing to work with these Senate members.

LOCALS OF MICHIGAN CITY WITH LARGEST MUSLIM POPULATION IN US CALL EL-SAYED ELECTION VICTORY 'NEEDED' CHANGE

"I'm very friendly with everyone," El-Sayed said. "Unless it's [Vice President] JD Vance."

Former Democratic adviser Dan Turrentine dismissed the significance of El-Sayed's language and jabs at Cruz, comparing the rhetoric to that of President Donald Trump.

"For starters, most Republicans would second that description of the senior Senator from Texas. But, if insults and crude nicknames prohibited working together, Trump would not work with several Republicans, including some in his cabinet, let alone Democrats. This will not impact El Sayed’s effectiveness whatsoever," Turrentine told Fox News Digital.
